title: Zechariah 9:9–17
context: Zion is called to rejoice because her King comes “lowly, and riding on a donkey”. The King brings peace to the nations and a dominion “from sea to sea”. Then the LORD frees prisoners “because of the blood of your covenant” and fights for his people against Greece. Matthew 21:5 and John 12:15 cite verse 9 at Jesus’ entry into Jerusalem; each Gospel quotes it in its own form, and readers can let each speak for itself. The Matthew 21:5 box treats that fulfillment. God’s promise to David in 2 Samuel 7 stands behind the royal hope as shared ground. Historic, symbolic, and future readings of the battle scenes appear in both traditions.

verses.text: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! Shout, daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your King comes to you! He is righteous, and having salvation; lowly, and riding on a donkey, even on a colt, the foal of a donkey.
verses.arminianNotes: “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion!” The King is “righteous, and having salvation; lowly”. Arminian readers hear the sincere “comes to you” as an invitation that Zion is meant to welcome, and see Jesus’ entry in the Gospels as this King’s coming.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same King and stress that his humility is the appointed path of God’s saving purpose, fulfilled at Jesus’ entry into Jerusalem. Shared ground: the King is righteous and lowly, the son promised to David in 2 Samuel 7, and both traditions adore him.

verses.text: I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem. The battle bow will be cut off; and he will speak peace to the nations. His dominion will be from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will cut off chariot, horse, and battle bow, and the King “will speak peace to the nations.” Arminian readers see a kingdom that spreads by peace rather than force, open to the nations, with a dominion reaching “to the ends of the earth.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see the King’s worldwide reign and often connect it with Christ’s rule through the gospel and its final completion. Shared ground: this King disarms war and rules all nations, and readers in both traditions differ on how much is present now and how much is future.

verses.text: As for you also, because of the blood of your covenant, I have set free your prisoners from the pit in which is no water.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD frees prisoners “because of the blood of your covenant,” recalling the covenant sealed with blood in Exodus 24. Arminian readers often connect this with the new covenant in Christ’s blood, while noting that the verse first addresses Zion’s captives.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear covenant blood as the basis of rescue and often read it in light of the Lord’s Supper words in the Gospels. Shared ground: God frees his people because of his covenant, not their merit, from a pit “in which is no water.”

verses.text: Turn to the stronghold, you prisoners of hope! Even today I declare that I will restore double to you.
verses.arminianNotes: “Turn to the stronghold, you prisoners of hope!” Arminian readers hear a real call to return, with the promise “I will restore double to you” encouraging captives to act on God’s word and come back.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same call and see the hope as anchored in God’s covenant faithfulness. Shared ground: those held captive are called “prisoners of hope”, because their future rests on the LORD’s promise to restore double.

verses.text: For indeed I bend Judah as a bow for me. I have loaded the bow with Ephraim. I will stir up your sons, Zion, against your sons, Greece, and will make you like the sword of a mighty man.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD bends Judah as a bow and loads it with Ephraim, stirring up Zion’s sons against “your sons, Greece”. Many interpreters connect this with later conflicts involving Greek powers, including the Maccabean period, while others read it as a broader picture; readers can hold the identification with care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also hold the historical identification loosely and note that Judah and Ephraim are reunited as one weapon in God’s hand. Shared ground: God uses his reunited people against oppressive powers, and the victory belongs to him rather than to their strength.

verses.text: The LORD will be seen over them. His arrow will flash like lightning. The Lord GOD will blow the trumpet, and will go with whirlwinds of the south.
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD will be seen over them”, his arrow flashing like lightning and the Lord GOD blowing the trumpet. Arminian readers see the imagery of a divine warrior, drawn from earlier pictures of God appearing in storm to fight for his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same theophany and stress that the battle is the LORD’s from start to finish. Shared ground: the whirlwinds of the south and the trumpet picture God going before his people, and the poetry should not be pressed into a battle plan.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies will defend them. They will destroy and overcome with sling stones. They will drink, and roar as through wine. They will be filled like bowls, like the corners of the altar.
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD of Armies will defend them.” The images of drinking, roaring, and bowls filled “like the corners of the altar” are vivid and debated; they may picture victory celebration or sacrificial abundance. Arminian readers leave the details open while keeping the theme of God’s defense.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also hold the imagery with care and note the link to the altar, which places the victory within worship. Shared ground: the LORD defends his people, and their triumph is pictured as a feast before him.

verses.text: The LORD their God will save them in that day as the flock of his people; for they are like the jewels of a crown, lifted on high over his land.
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD their God will save them in that day as the flock of his people”. Arminian readers see the tender picture of a shepherd saving his flock, with his people valued “like the jewels of a crown”.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same picture and stress that God saves his people as his own possession. Shared ground: the shepherd image prepares for chapter 10, and those he saves are lifted high over his land like jewels in a crown.

verses.text: For how great is his goodness, and how great is his beauty! Grain will make the young men flourish, and new wine the virgins.
verses.arminianNotes: “For how great is his goodness, and how great is his beauty!” Arminian readers see the oracle ending in praise, with grain and new wine picturing renewed blessing for young men and women in a restored land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see the chapter closing in wonder at God’s goodness. Interpreters differ on whether “his” refers to God, to the people, or to the land. Shared ground: the restored people flourish because the LORD is good, and the right response is praise.
